sources.note: Local machine transcript (faster-whisper), no speaker labels; Dex, Vaibhav, Viv (LangChain) and Jeff (Ralph loop) speak; attributed by content. README also read. Listed in inventory line 136.

sources.title: AI That Works #40: Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
sources.note: Local machine transcript (faster-whisper), no speaker labels; Dex, Vaibhav, guest Mike; attributed by content. README also read. Listed in inventory line 158.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: harness engineering is not like how do you build a harness
cards.claim: Dex defines harness engineering as engineering on top of the harness you are given (configuration surface of Claude Code: CLAUDE.md, skills, MCP) with a systems and context-engineering approach, not building a harness.
cards.evidence_detail: Definition stated in discussion; no data.
cards.landing: Frames the whole harness work as configuration engineering; supports skills/agent packages as the surface to tune.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: extension points, right? So you have MCPs and CloudMD
cards.claim: Dex describes what a harness adds over a raw agent loop as extension points (CLAUDE.md loading, skill files, built-in MCP, context compression) that pull things from the environment into the system prompt or tools.
cards.evidence_detail: Whiteboard explanation; no data.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md and skills are the harness extension points; sets what counts as harness config in the repo.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: harness engineering is only genuinely new when you're RLing a model on a specific set of tools
cards.claim: Dex says the genuinely new thing in harness engineering is RL-training a model on a specific tool set (apply-patch vs old-string/new-string), which is where product advantage lies, and that this does not apply to teams configuring a vendor harness.
cards.evidence_detail: Claims Claude-code models do badly in the Codex harness and gpt-oss-120b cannot do old-string/new-string; no numbers.
cards.landing: Nowhere obvious; argues that FixFlow should not build its own harness, only tune config.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the outer harness may not even look anything like the inner harness
cards.claim: Dex distinguishes an inner harness (model plus tools) from an outer harness (even a bash while-true loop or orchestrator) and notes the dumbest outer loop (Ralph) still works well.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual; Ralph cited as working.
cards.landing: The Workflow-tool scripts are the outer harness; supports saving them as a library.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: building deterministic or non-deterministic code around a good harness is incredibly powerful
cards.claim: Dex endorses wrapping deterministic or non-deterministic orchestration code around a good vendor harness as a high-leverage move, using Ralph as the proof that a trivial orchestration layer pays.
cards.evidence_detail: Ralph loop cited; no measurements.
cards.landing: Supports script-level orchestration around the phase routine rather than prose-only compliance.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: These context windows are good for one goal, one activity with the right context
cards.claim: Dex says the fundamental that made agents good is one goal per context window, with Claude Code continually recycling contexts.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as fundamental; no data.
cards.landing: Backs the one-phase-per-new-session routine.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can always do more context engineering on top of a new model release
cards.claim: Dex's answer to the bitter lesson is surfing the models: new releases make prior code irrelevant but you can immediately do more context engineering and stay 5-10 percent ahead; the principles persist.
cards.evidence_detail: Credits Dan Shipper's term 'surfing the models'; the 5-10 percent figure is an estimate, unmeasured.
cards.landing: Argues for re-auditing CLAUDE.md and routing on each model release rather than freezing config.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you have good evals, the new code is cheap to write
cards.claim: Dex argues that code written around a model is cheap to throw away if you have a decent eval, so the eval is the durable asset and the eval acts as the deterministic spec (auto research loop).
cards.evidence_detail: Argument; references auto research without data.
cards.landing: P1 cold-resume trial as a durable eval for the harness; keep evals, expect to rewrite routine text.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: people just say 'Claude, figure it out' and never look at what's coming back
cards.claim: Dex warns that the common failure in context, harness and eval-loop work is never looking at the data, and says do not spend a week automating what takes five seconds by hand.
cards.evidence_detail: Says he sees it 'all the time'; no counts.
cards.landing: Argues for reading transcripts of the first routine runs before adding compliance machinery.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Don't write a git patch man
cards.claim: Dex says a model trained on one harness's tool format is poor in another, so tool formats are harness-specific and cannot be swapped freely.
cards.evidence_detail: Claims Claude-code models are 'complete trash' in the Codex harness; no numbers.
cards.landing: Nowhere obvious; caution when porting skills/agents across harnesses.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: exhaust all the avenues in this, like, intelligence one stack before you even think about
cards.claim: Co-guest Viv argues, and Dex does not dispute, that one should exhaust the single-loop stack (system prompt, tool design, context funnelling, skills) before adding another orchestration loop; Vaibhav counters that nested loops buy speed.
cards.evidence_detail: Position in debate; Dex's own stance partly shown by his single-loop-first framing.
cards.landing: Tension with multi-agent workflow scripts: tune the single agent's instructions first.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you need to constantly be trying things that you don't think will work
cards.claim: Dex endorses Simon Willison's advice to keep trying dumb or futuristic things to keep your model-capability understanding current, and that flexibility beats locking in a workflow.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites Simon; also Jeff says it is too soon to lock in loops/workflows.
cards.landing: Warns against freezing a workflow library early.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: other
cards.quote: overfit to the entire email set. And this will completely not generalize
cards.claim: Guest warns that auto-research outputs can overfit (60 enumerated if-else cases in the prompt, like benchmark cheating), so look at them yourself; Dex responds that production data and a human in the loop are needed.
cards.evidence_detail: Anecdote about auto-research prompts and Terminal-Bench cheating; no numbers.
cards.landing: Caution for any automated tuning of CLAUDE.md or skills against a small eval set.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every team that doesn't have an AI code review bar is freaking dumb
cards.claim: Dex states that every team should have an AI code review bot in the PR flow, calling it an objectively right take.
cards.evidence_detail: Said in passing on a no-sponsors show; names CodeRabbit as the one they use.
cards.landing: Matches the Opus reviewer per PR; no change.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Every engineer needs to build an agent and do their first tool registration
cards.claim: Dex (with Jeff) holds every engineer should hand-build an agent loop and read Claude Code/Codex source, since sub-agents, delegation of command-safety checks to Haiku and context recycling are the techniques to understand before relying on higher-level harnesses.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion; the Haiku safety delegation example is from the source leak, unquantified.
cards.landing: Supports the Haiku locator agent pattern and cheap-model delegation for sub-tasks.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: design it so it's easy to delete
cards.claim: Dex endorses designing so capabilities are easy to delete when the model improves and being careful what you expose as a product substrate, to avoid accumulating tech debt.
cards.evidence_detail: Principle; no data.
cards.landing: Argues skill and agent packages should be small and removable, and that CLAUDE.md rules be re-justified each model release.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: harness engineering is all about wrapping the model to do useful work
cards.claim: Dex adopts the practical recipe of an unopinionated harness plus task plus production traces as an eval set, fit the harness (skills, system prompt, context) to the evals and then review it as a human, and says the easiest leverage is editing the harness.
cards.evidence_detail: Recommendation; Dex says he is bullish on auto-research and evals encoding behaviour.
cards.landing: Use real session transcripts as the eval set for CLAUDE.md and skills tuning.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the wild loop having a human in the loop is a great process
cards.claim: Dex agrees a human in the loop inside the outer loop is a good way to inject intelligence, and warns against over-engineering automation of small tasks.
cards.evidence_detail: Brief agreement; no data.
cards.landing: Supports owner checkpoints in the phase routine over full automation.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every feature has a metric tied to it
cards.claim: Dex tells (as an analogy from Google/Facebook deploys) that an agent loop needs a prod metric and gradual rollout with a human watching at release, since without prod data you overfit to the wrong thing.
cards.evidence_detail: Recollection of 2015-era deploy practice; paraphrase of the speaker; no numbers.
cards.landing: Nowhere obvious; supports a measurement-first gate before the dispatcher switch-on.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you probably don't need an agent if you know the workflow order
cards.claim: Dex says control flow written as prompt instructions (control flow via prompt) is a mistake: if you know the order, use a script, as a make-task agent needed two hours of added instructions where a 90-second bash script sufficed.
cards.evidence_detail: Own anecdote: 2 hours vs 90 seconds, one project.
cards.landing: Phase routine steps that are fixed could be script/hook-driven instead of prose the agent must self-report.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't use prompts for control flow
cards.claim: Dex's headline takeaway: do not use prompts for control flow; start broad and robust, learn actual inputs, add more deterministic happy paths and keep a fully agentic escape hatch.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing takeaway; backed by the make-file anecdote.
cards.landing: Direct pressure on a self-reported phase routine; favours encoding steps in scripts or hooks.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the model would basically skip steps
cards.claim: Dex reports that with the create-plan prompt customers rushed and the model skipped the early design-question and outline phases, which are what make the plan good; without them the plan is little better than 'go write the code'.
cards.evidence_detail: Customer observation; no rate given.
cards.landing: Evidence that a prose phase routine is skipped under pressure; matches W2 (skipped looks like unconsulted).

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: frontier thingy allums can fall about 150 to 200
cards.claim: Dex cites Kyle's study that frontier LLMs follow roughly 150-200 instructions reliably (as of about mid-2026 minus six months, probably higher now) and says the create-plan prompt holds over a hundred, repeated and in caps.
cards.evidence_detail: Figure 150-200 instructions from Kyle Mistele's CLAUDE.md post study, recalled by Dex as six or seven months old; his own count of 'over a hundred' is an estimate.
cards.landing: Instruction-count basis for the 390-line CLAUDE.md trim; note he says the limit is probably higher now.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every time you put in all caps, like you must important, critical, never
cards.claim: Dex says emphatic caps (must, critical, never) do not buy compliance because the model can attend to only so many instructions; split the prompt into separate smaller workflows instead.
cards.evidence_detail: Explanation; no measurement.
cards.landing: Argues against the MUST/Never emphasis style in CLAUDE.md invariants; split by phase.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: short back and forth which are still very early in the context window
cards.claim: Dex explains why design questions come before the plan: feedback early in the context is high leverage, whereas after a 1000-line plan (5-10 percent of context) most attention is on the model's own decisions and feedback is low leverage and degrades toward the dumb zone.
cards.evidence_detail: Plan size stated as ~1000 lines, 5-10 percent of context; no experiment.
cards.landing: Supports questions-before-plan ordering and fresh session per phase.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: editing with consistency is a much harder task than creating with consistency
cards.claim: Editing a plan after feedback in the same context yields inconsistent partial application; when a fast one-shot plan is not ~95 percent right, delete it and restart down the interactive path rather than re-steer.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's observation, Dex agrees; '95 percent' is a rule of thumb.
cards.landing: Restart-over-repair rule for plans; fits one phase per new session.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're forcing the compaction workflows in between
cards.claim: Dex's structured-planning SDK splits one big prompt into design, structure and plan agents with schema-typed outputs and deterministic code between phases, forcing intentional compaction at phase boundaries instead of relying on users to know when to start fresh.
cards.evidence_detail: Live demo (alpha); the exit condition is an empty open-questions array.
cards.landing: Exit conditions as structured data checked by code is a model for hook-checked phase gates.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have an outer harness, which is like, okay, cool, like all questions answered
cards.claim: Dex's design has an inner Claude-Code loop per phase and an outer deterministic harness that checks the structured output (all questions answered) before moving to a different prompt built for the next phase.
cards.evidence_detail: Demo with SDK; also done with BAML parse step as alternative to built-in structured output.
cards.landing: Pattern for a phase runner that verifies phase completion from output, not from the agent's report.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: enforcing a style guide that says if you're going to use a coding agent
cards.claim: Dex endorses a more opinionated coding agent that forces a process, making the default path the correct one, and a junior gets better consistency from robust steps than generic Claude Code.
cards.evidence_detail: Endorses Vaibhav's style-guide framing; no data.
cards.landing: Supports making the phase routine the default via commands/skills rather than prose.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have like five, six slices of the original three prompts
cards.claim: Dex changes his research-plan-implement split: an internal five- or six-step version (questions, objective research, design discussion, outline, plan) breaks compaction up further, but costs users six slash commands to learn, so the UI should show the next step rather than force it.
cards.evidence_detail: Internal practice; no results.
cards.landing: Phase granularity trade-off: more phases mean more commands to learn; have the tool suggest next step.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: plans sucked. They're actually too long
cards.claim: Dex retracts plan review as the mental-alignment artifact: plans are too long to review (250 lines of code per phase), so the team moved back to reviewing the structure outline, the plan's overview without code.
cards.evidence_detail: Change of position; owner review practice; no numbers beyond the 250-line example.
cards.landing: Owner review should target the outline/Plan @ sha summary, not the full plan body.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can give that to Haiku, it can tell you if there's open questions
cards.claim: Dex (with Vaibhav) notes a 500-line design doc can be run through a cheap model (Haiku) with a simple structured-output prompt to detect open questions, so gating checks do not need the frontier model.
cards.evidence_detail: Claim in discussion; not measured.
cards.landing: Cheap-model checker for phase-complete gates, consistent with the Haiku locator agent.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: just doing constant re-research in the back background while everything else is running
cards.claim: Dex likes the idea of a background verifier or re-researcher that runs while the human proceeds down the golden path and interrupts only when it finds a problem; design what is fast, slow, synchronous or background.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says he had not thought of it and likes it; takeaways closing the show.
cards.landing: Background verifier pattern for the review stage without blocking the main session.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: other
cards.quote: have fewer steps or have a more accurate step selection system
cards.claim: Vaibhav (Dex agrees, restating context-length and accuracy levers) says only two levers improve an agent system, fewer steps or more accurate step selection, and per-step error compounds (99 percent over 20 steps veers off).
cards.evidence_detail: Compounding illustrated with a chart (99 percent accuracy, 20 steps); the 60 percent figure for 50 steps is stated loosely.
cards.landing: Fewer steps in a phase beats adding judges; argues against growing step counts in the routine.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can wrap it in a deterministic harness of like it's either run once or run forever
cards.claim: Dex shows a Ralph loop built in the SDK where a structured output decides whether the exit condition has been met, instead of a bare bash loop.
cards.evidence_detail: Demo; burrito SaaS toy task.
cards.landing: Exit-condition-as-typed-output for any loop-style workflow script.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: other
cards.quote: the more I codified it, the less other people wanted to do it
cards.claim: Guest Mike reports that a heavily codified research-plan-implement process lowered team adoption because people wanted their own way, and Dex's team coaching relies on reading threads to teach; Dex hosts and endorses revisiting in a month.
cards.evidence_detail: One team of 25 engineers; the tool was 24 hours old.
cards.landing: Adoption risk of a prescriptive routine for any additional humans; one owner today.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: other
cards.quote: JSON versus Markdown a lot... a status enum like to do in progress done
cards.claim: A guest keeps the plan state in a PRD.json with a todo/in-progress/done status enum so deterministic code, not the model, orchestrates which story runs next; Dex gives the reason that deterministic code reads it.
cards.evidence_detail: Guest's tool, 24 hours old; Dex only glosses the rationale.
cards.landing: Machine-readable phase state beside the markdown plan.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: other
cards.quote: every build step that you run needs to run warning free
cards.claim: Vaibhav enforces zero build warnings at compile time to cut context bloat from noisy build output, plus dependency-boundary checks in CI/pre-commit and a diffable dependency-graph visual reviewed in PRs.
cards.evidence_detail: BAML team practice; no numbers.
cards.landing: Backpressure: warning-free builds and import-boundary checks reduce output noise; FixFlow already has import-linter in CI.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: design docs leave outside of our code base, because code evolves much faster than design
cards.claim: Vaibhav argues design docs are time-stamped checkpoints that may live outside the repo, with an AI pass verifying every review comment was addressed; Dex frames the SDLC shift as moving human leverage upstream to thinking and design.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion; markdown-with-comments tool is in use at BAML for two weeks.
cards.landing: Tension with keeping decisions in-repo; the PR body journal is a checkpoint, not a living spec.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #40 Applying 12-Factor Principles to Coding Agent SDKs
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: he gets a message in Slack saying, hey, all comments are taken care of
cards.claim: Dex's closing: if the user experience is a tight loop keep it fast and push heavy verification to background tasks; a rewritten workflow should ask what is synchronous, asynchronous or background (the guest's design-comment verifier does that).
cards.evidence_detail: Final takeaways; attribution of the Slack example is to the Vaibhav side.
cards.landing: Verifier runs async and reports; owner view stays one page.

gaps: Both are machine transcripts without speaker labels; in the harness-engineering episode several positions (nested while loops, evals-as-spec disagreement) are split between Dex, Vaibhav, Viv and Jeff and attribution is by content, so some cards are marked other or Dex+others.

No Dex measurements in either episode; the only numbers are the 150-200 instruction figure (Kyle's study), a 90-second vs 2-hour anecdote, 99 percent over 20 steps compounding, and plan size of about 1000 lines.
The harness-engineering transcript has no discussion of hooks, MCP debate detail, or skills beyond one mention; Viv's screen-shared post was not audible/legible in the transcript.
The speaker who uses Claude Code's 'Explore/plan tool and Haiku for is-this-command-safe' is probably Jeff, not Dex; carded under Dex only as an endorsed practice.

new_sources.title: Kyle Mistele, writing a good CLAUDE.md (instruction-following study cited at 150-200 instructions)
new_sources.why: Dex cites this study as the origin of the instruction-count limit; likely a primary source for W1.

new_sources.title: Ralph Wiggum agent loop session (AI That Works 2025-10-28)
new_sources.why: Linked in the harness-engineering README as the basis for the outer-loop argument.
